entry.title: A randomized U.S. survey shows that a strong warning about student AI use lowered hiring professionals’ ratings of hypothetical graduates; it measured neither actual hires nor wages.
A London matched-application experiment found a pooled interview-invitation lift from an AI-related certificate for underrepresented women, but not parity, hiring or wage gains.
Danish firms first reporting AI use showed slower hiring relative to trend, mainly at small firms; this is an observational gap, not a layoff count.
A Danish study found no extra early-career-share decline at workplaces encouraging chatbots through 2024; it is the same underlying study already tracked, not a new replication.
A Federal Reserve manufacturing note finds broad AI skills in ads and a large unadjusted posted-pay gap; it does not show worker raises, hires or layoffs.
Added full-paper evidence that U.S. vacancy exposure changed through both the mix of posted roles and listed tasks within comparable groups; this is not an AI-caused job-loss estimate.

A U.S. startup study reports that more entry offset jobs lost at exposed incumbents without raising aggregate startup employment; a UK entry null narrows generalization of the prior startup-growth signal.
Added a CEPR startup-entry counter-signal: more entry and reported industry-level labor growth in more GenAI-exposed industries, with causal and coverage limits explicit.
Added a Census validation: exposure scores predict reported firm AI use only partly, so exposure-based job warnings are not proof of employer adoption or AI-caused losses.
Added a U.S. software-vacancy study: junior ads fell roughly 14–15% relative to senior ads after ChatGPT, but the study does not establish AI-caused hires or job losses.
Added a methodological test: platform conversation shares can change U.S. employment coefficients even when the labor-market design is fixed. This does not estimate AI-caused job loss.

Added a controlled pitch-screening study: ChatGPT assistance reduced pooled accuracy in identifying experience on average but improved it for some non-English-speaking writers. This is not a measured hiring or employment effect.

Added a Cleveland Fed working paper showing higher advertised pay but lower incumbent pay in more LLM-exposed U.S. occupations. The answer now separates job ads, realized wages and worker status without claiming a causal AI effect.

Added a randomized Philippine interview-stage study: AI voice interviews increased offers at one recruiter, while human hiring decisions remained. The answer now separates application barriers, interview outcomes and net jobs.

Added a formal model of AI-assisted applications and hiring: less informative written materials can make employers rely more on prior experience, creating a possible entry barrier. The current answer now separates this mechanism from evidence of real screening, hiring or employment changes.

Added a U.S. advertised-pay result: highly AI-exposed occupations posted faster pay growth while their entry-level share shrank. The current answer now separates a seniority-shift warning from actual wages, AI adoption and a broad employment verdict.

Added a Texas administrative-record study: graduates from more AI-exposed majors had lower first-year Texas employment and earnings after ChatGPT. The current answer now separates a second entry-level warning from employer adoption, graduate unemployment and a broad U.S. verdict.

Added a 41-country adoption-linked study: AI-adopting multinational affiliates shifted toward senior workers, with a 1.9-point lower junior share by March 2026. The current answer now separates a workforce-composition warning from a mass-layoff claim and the broad U.S. null.

Added Yale Budget Lab’s update through August 2026: its broad U.S. tracker still finds no clear AI labor-market footprint. The current answer now separates that aggregate counter-signal from unresolved early-career and regional warnings.

Added a quasi-experimental Swedish AI-grant study: awarded firms posted more vacancies, especially white-collar vacancies, while the study did not detect effects on total employment, hiring or separations. The current answer now separates job ads from completed hiring and headcount.
